target: AG1's claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels because some countries already have very high renewable electricity shares
objection: AG2 argued that the United States has never historically exceeded 20% alternative energy use, and that a true replacement of fossil fuels would require supplying the majority of the energy services fossil fuels currently provide, not just a small slice of electricity.

target: AG1's implication that alternative energies alone can replace fossil fuels without a transition fuel
objection: AG2 argued that because alternative energies have not shown they can provide the majority of the energy services fossil fuels supply in a large country like the U.S., natural gas is still appropriate and necessary as a bridge fuel to reach net-zero.

target: AG2's use of the U.S. historical alternative-energy share as evidence that alternatives cannot replace fossil fuels
objection: AG1 objected that a low historical U.S. alternative-energy share does not by itself prove that alternative energies cannot effectively replace fossil fuels, especially since the necessary knowledge and tools already exist to transition away from fossil fuels.

target: AG2's claim that natural gas is necessary because only alternatives plus nuclear cannot end fossil-fuel dependence quickly
objection: AG1 argued that nuclear energy is a low-carbon alternative that is the quickest way to end dependence on fossil fuels and uses far less land than renewables, so including nuclear in alternative-energy portfolios can accelerate replacement without needing natural gas as a required bridge.

target: AG2's broader claim that alternatives cannot effectively replace fossil fuels at national scale
objection: AG1 cited real grids in Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway with very high renewable shares to show that alternative energies can supply the vast majority of national electricity demand in functioning, real-world power systems, thereby displacing fossil-fuel electricity at national scale.

target: AG2's assumption that replacing fossil fuels requires simultaneously replacing every fossil-fuel end use at once
objection: AG1 argued that energy transitions can be phased, and that an effective near-to-medium-term replacement strategy does not need to replace every fossil-fuel service instantly; decarbonizing electricity first is a viable first step because electrification can then reduce fossil-fuel use in heating, transport, and some industry.

target: AG2's claim that renewables and other alternatives cannot meet dispatchable reliability requirements
objection: AG1 replied that nuclear can provide firm, dispatchable low-carbon electricity, and that variable renewables can be paired with hydropower and long-duration storage, so alternative-energy portfolios can meet reliability needs rather than depending on fossil backup.

target: AG2's claim that nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective to serve as a serious firm low-carbon substitute
objection: AG1 implicitly rejected the idea that nuclear must be dismissed on safety and effectiveness grounds, instead treating nuclear as a practical firm low-carbon option that can help replace fossil fuels quickly and with much less land use than renewables.

target: AG2's claim that grid firming resources like hydropower and long-duration storage cannot scale fast enough in large countries
objection: AG1 pointed to already-operating national systems with very high renewable shares as evidence that non-fossil firming and demand-matching capacity can scale in practice, so the alleged build-out barrier is not necessarily decisive and does not force reliance on fossil backup.

target: AG1's reliance on high-renewable electricity systems as proof that fossil fuels can be fully replaced
objection: AG2 countered that this only addresses electricity, while fossil fuels also provide broader energy services such as heating, transport fuels, and industrial energy; therefore high-renewable electricity alone does not show fossil fuels can be effectively replaced across the whole energy system.

target: AG1's assumption that decarbonized electricity automatically eliminates fossil-fuel dependence
objection: AG2 argued that many non-electric fossil-fuel uses cannot be switched instantly to alternative electricity at the needed scale because end-use technologies and infrastructure change more slowly than power generation, so fossil fuels can remain necessary during the transition even if the grid is decarbonized.

target: AG1's claim that natural gas is not necessary as a bridge fuel if alternative energies can replace fossil electricity
objection: AG2 maintained that natural gas remains an appropriate and necessary bridge because it can preserve reliable energy service while other fossil-fuel end uses transition more slowly, so alternatives alone cannot yet effectively replace fossil fuels overall.

target: AG1's assumption that existing renewable and firming technologies can cover dispatchable reliability without fossil backup
objection: AG2 argued that effective replacement requires low-carbon sources that can provide dispatchable reliability during peak demand and low renewable output, but many firming options—especially hydropower and long-duration storage—face site, hydrology, engineering, permitting, and build-time constraints that prevent assuming they will scale fast enough in time.

target: AG1's reliance on nuclear as a safe, firm substitute
objection: AG2 argued that nuclear should not be treated as a risk-free firm low-carbon option because accidents such as Fukushima can wipe out carbon-free electricity gains and undermine reliability, making nuclear too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious global-warming solution.

target: AG1's claim that alternative-energy portfolios can reliably meet dispatchable demand on their own
objection: AG2 argued that because renewable output is variable and firming capacity cannot be assumed to scale quickly enough, alternative-energy portfolios alone cannot be relied on to supply dispatchable reliability throughout the transition without dispatchable fossil backup.
